lessons.title: Introduction to Tags

sections.content: HTML, or HyperText Markup Language, is the standard language used to create and structure content on the web. Every webpage you visit — from a simple blog to a complex web application — is built on a foundation of HTML. Without HTML, browsers would have no idea how to display text, images, or links.

sections.title: Did you know?
sections.content: HTML is NOT a programming language — it's a markup language. It tells the browser how to display content, but it doesn't perform calculations or logic. That's what JavaScript is for!

Every HTML document follows a standard structure. The DOCTYPE declaration tells the browser which version of HTML you're using, and the rest organizes your content into head (metadata) and body (visible content).

This is my first webpage.

sections.content: HTML is made up of elements. An element usually has an opening tag, some content, and a closing tag. Tags are keywords surrounded by angle brackets. Most tags come in pairs — the closing tag has a forward slash before the keyword.

sections.content: HTML is the entry point into web development. Before you can style a page with CSS or add interactivity with JavaScript, you need a solid HTML structure. Think of HTML as the skeleton — it gives everything else something to attach to.

objectives: Understand what HTML is and its role in web development
Learn the basic structure of an HTML document
Identify and use common HTML tags like headings and paragraphs
Write a simple working webpage from scratch
lessons.mentorTip: Don't worry about memorizing every HTML tag. Start with the basics — headings, paragraphs, and links — and build from there. You will naturally learn more tags as you build real projects.

lessons.title: Data & Validation

sections.content: Forms are how websites collect input from users — whether logging in, submitting feedback, or filling out a contact form. In HTML, the <form> element wraps all form controls, and attributes like action and method define where and how data is sent.

sections.title: Pro Tip
sections.content: Always connect every <input> with a corresponding <label> using the 'for' attribute matching the input's 'id'. This improves user accessibility and touch targets!
The <input> element is versatile. By changing its type attribute, you can accept text, passwords, emails, numbers, checkboxes, and radio buttons.

sections.code:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
  <!-- Text Input -->
  <label for="username">Username:</label>
  <input type="text" id="username" name="username" required>

  <!-- Email Input -->
  <label for="email">Email:</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>

  <!-- Password Input -->
  <label for="pwd">Password:</label>
  <input type="password" id="pwd" name="password" minlength="6" required>

  <!-- Submit Button -->
  <button type="submit">Register</button>
</form>

sections.content: HTML provides native client-side validation attributes like required, minlength, maxlength, min, max, and pattern. The browser checks these before the form is submitted, showing warning messages automatically.

sections.code:
<!-- Required number input between 18 and 99 -->
<label for="age">Age:</label>
<input type="number" id="age" name="age" min="18" max="99" required>

<!-- Custom pattern validation for phone numbers -->
<label for="phone">Phone (digits only):</label>
<input type="tel" id="phone" name="phone" pattern="[0-9]{10}">

objectives: Understand common input types: text, email, password, number, and tel
Implement HTML native validation with required, min, max, and pattern attributes
Learn best practices for accessible form design
lessons.mentorTip: HTML native validation is fast and works without any JavaScript. Use built-in input types like email and number to get mobile browser keyboard optimizations automatically!
